title: Health and safety at work
blurb: Apply HASAWA, RIDDOR, COSHH, manual handling rules, LOLER and the Sharps Regulations to everyday nursing.
question: A healthcare assistant hurts her back while repositioning a patient and is unable to do her normal duties for nine days. Is this reportable under RIDDOR, and within what time?

teach.h: Health and safety law in one sentence
teach.body: Health and safety law makes employers and employees jointly responsible for keeping work safe. Under section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (HASAWA), every employee must take reasonable care for their own health and safety and that of others affected by what they do or fail to do, and must cooperate with the employer. In plain English: follow the safe systems your employer sets up, and do not put yourself, patients or colleagues at risk.

items: RIDDOR 2013: certain work injuries, diseases and dangerous occurrences must be reported to the HSE.
COSHH 2002: substances hazardous to health (cleaning agents, disinfectants) are assessed and controlled.
Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992: avoid, assess, reduce.
LOLER 1998: lifting equipment, including hoists and slings, is thoroughly examined at set intervals.
Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013: safer sharps and no recapping.

steps.label: Avoid
steps.sub: hazardous manual handling, so far as reasonably practicable

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: the risk of any handling that cannot be avoided

steps.label: Reduce
steps.sub: the risk to as low as reasonably practicable

teach.caption: The law sets no specific weight limits. A load can be an object, person or animal (HSE, Manual handling at work).

items.label: LOLER thorough examination: people-lifting equipment and accessories (hoists, slings)
RIDDOR: deaths and specified injuries, report without delay

teach.caption: LOLER intervals apply unless an examination scheme specifies otherwise.

teach.h: Is a worker's injury reportable under RIDDOR?

children.label: Report within 15 days of the accident

teach.caption: The 7 days do not count the day of the accident but do include weekends and rest days.

head: Specified injury
Detail
rows: Any bone except fingers, thumbs and toes
Arm, hand, finger, thumb, leg, foot or toe
Over 10% of body surface, or to eyes or airway
Permanent loss or reduction of sight
teach.caption: HSE, Specified injuries to workers (RIDDOR 2013).

teach.body: COSHH requires hazardous substances to be assessed with control measures set out; the safety data sheet and COSHH assessment tell you the dilution, ventilation and PPE to use. Follow them and do not mix products. The Sharps Regulations 2013 require unnecessary sharps to be avoided, safer sharps used as designed, no recapping, and disposal at the point of use. Report every sharps injury and near miss.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Kofi on a medical ward
teach.body: Kofi slips on a spill in the sluice on Tuesday and fractures his wrist. A wrist fracture is a specified injury (not a finger, thumb or toe), so the trust must report it to the HSE without delay and within 10 days. Kofi makes the area safe for others first, gets his wrist assessed, and completes the trust incident report and accident record. His manager reviews why the spill was left, so the hazard is controlled for everyone.

teach.text: Over-7-day means MORE than seven consecutive days off normal work, not counting the accident day but counting weekends. It is reported within 15 days. Do not confuse it with the 10-day limit for specified injuries and deaths.

items: HASAWA s7: take reasonable care of yourself and others, and cooperate with your employer.
Manual handling: avoid, assess, reduce; no legal weight limits.
LOLER: hoists and slings examined at least every 6 months; take faulty or out-of-date equipment out of use.
RIDDOR: deaths and specified injuries within 10 days; over-7-day injuries within 15 days.
COSHH: follow the assessment and data sheet. Sharps: no recapping, dispose at the point of use.

summary: You can now state the employee's duties under HASAWA s7 and apply manual handling, LOLER, COSHH and sharps rules to ward situations. You can also decide whether a worker's injury is reportable under RIDDOR and within what time.

A.q: A newly registered nurse asks what section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires of her. Which answer is correct?
options: Take reasonable care of herself and others, and cooperate
Write and review the ward's own risk assessments
Report all injuries at work directly to the HSE by herself
Provide personal protective equipment for her colleagues
A.why: Section 7 places two duties on employees: take reasonable care for their own health and safety and that of others affected by their acts or omissions, and cooperate with the employer (HASAWA 1974).

whyNot.1: Writing risk assessments is an employer duty that may be delegated; it is not the s7 employee duty.
whyNot.2: RIDDOR reports are made by the employer as the responsible person; employees report through local systems.
whyNot.3: Providing PPE is an employer responsibility; employees must use it as instructed.

A.q: Under the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992, what is the first step in managing a hazardous manual handling task?
options: Assess the risk of injury from the whole task
Avoid it so far as is reasonably practicable
Reduce the risk with lifting equipment
Train staff to lift within the safe weight limits
A.why: The hierarchy is avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable, then assess what cannot be avoided, then reduce the risk to as low as reasonably practicable (HSE).

whyNot.0: Assessment comes second, for handling that cannot be avoided.
whyNot.2: Reducing risk is the third step, after avoiding and assessing.
whyNot.3: The law sets no specific weight limits, and training is part of reducing risk, not the first step.

A.q: How often must a patient hoist sling be thoroughly examined under LOLER 1998, unless an examination scheme says otherwise?
options: At least every 3 months
At least every 6 months
At least every 12 months
At least every 24 months
A.why: Equipment and accessories used for lifting people, such as hoists and slings, need a thorough examination at least every 6 months; other lifting equipment every 12 months (HSE, LOLER).

whyNot.0: Three months is more frequent than the LOLER minimum for people-lifting equipment.
whyNot.2: Twelve months applies to lifting equipment that does not lift people.
whyNot.3: Twenty-four months is not a LOLER interval for lifting equipment.

B.q: A healthcare assistant injures her shoulder at work and cannot do her normal duties for 10 days. Within what time must this be reported under RIDDOR?
options: Within 15 days of the accident
Within 10 days of the accident
Within 7 days of the accident
Within 30 days of the accident
B.why: An injury that stops a worker doing normal work for more than seven consecutive days (excluding the accident day, including weekends) must be reported within 15 days of the accident (RIDDOR 2013).

whyNot.1: Ten days is the limit for deaths and specified injuries.
whyNot.2: Seven days is the incapacity threshold, not the reporting deadline.
whyNot.3: Thirty days is longer than the RIDDOR limit for over-7-day injuries.

B.q: A porter slips on a wet ward floor and fractures his ankle. How should this be reported under RIDDOR?
options: As an over-7-day injury within 15 days
As a near miss on the local reporting system
As a specified injury, within 10 days
As a dangerous occurrence within 30 days
B.why: A fracture other than to fingers, thumbs or toes is a specified injury. Specified injuries must be reported without delay and within 10 days (HSE, RIDDOR 2013). It is also recorded locally.

whyNot.0: The 15-day route is for over-7-day injuries; a specified injury is reported sooner.
whyNot.1: A fracture is an actual injury, not a near miss, and it is reportable to the HSE.
whyNot.3: A dangerous occurrence is a listed near-miss event; this is an injury to a worker.

B.q: A new disinfectant is delivered to the ward. A colleague plans to make it stronger than the label says because the ward is busy. What should the nurse advise?
options: Use a stronger dilution if gloves are worn
Mix it with the usual ward detergent to save time
Use it neat on surfaces that are visibly dirty
Follow its COSHH assessment for dilution and PPE
B.why: COSHH 2002 requires hazardous substances to be assessed with control measures set. Staff must follow the assessment and safety data sheet for dilution, ventilation and PPE (HSE, COSHH basics; HASAWA s7 cooperation).

whyNot.0: Gloves do not make an unassessed concentration safe; the stated dilution and controls apply.
whyNot.1: Mixing products can create hazardous reactions and is outside the assessed controls.
whyNot.2: Using it neat departs from the COSHH assessment and may harm staff and patients.

C.q: Lena, a nurse, sprains her wrist at work on Friday 1 March. She is unable to do her normal work from Saturday 2 March to Monday 11 March inclusive. What does RIDDOR require?
options: Not reportable, as weekend days are excluded from the count
Report by 11 March as a specified injury
Report by 16 March as an over-7-day injury
Report by 31 March as a reportable disease
C.why: Not counting the accident day but including weekends, she is off normal work for 10 consecutive days, which is more than 7. An over-7-day injury must be reported within 15 days of the accident: 1 March plus 15 days is 16 March (RIDDOR 2013).

whyNot.0: Weekends and rest days are included when counting the 7 days.
whyNot.1: A sprain is not a specified injury; specified injuries include fractures other than fingers, thumbs and toes.
whyNot.3: A sprain is an injury, not an occupational disease, and the deadline is 15 days.

C.q: A nurse traps her finger in a door, fracturing it. She returns to normal duties the next morning. What is the correct action?
options: Record it locally; it is not RIDDOR-reportable
Report it to the HSE as a specified injury
Report it to the HSE within 15 days
Report it to the HSE as a dangerous occurrence
C.why: Fractures of fingers, thumbs and toes are excluded from specified injuries, and she was not off normal work for more than 7 days. It is therefore not reportable under RIDDOR, but it should be recorded locally (HSE).

whyNot.1: Finger fractures are specifically excluded from the specified injury list.
whyNot.2: The 15-day route needs more than 7 days off normal work, which did not happen.
whyNot.3: A trapped finger is an injury, not a listed dangerous occurrence.

C.q: On a busy medicines round, Hannah sees a student nurse recap a used insulin needle so she can carry it to the treatment room. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask the student to hand the needle to her for disposal
Remind her to recap it one-handed to avoid an injury
Let it pass and raise it in her end-of-placement feedback
Ask her to bin it at the point of use, then explain why
C.why: The Sharps Regulations 2013 require no recapping and disposal at the point of use by the user. Hannah should stop the unsafe practice now and then teach the reason: Code 19.4 (avoid health risks to colleagues and others) and 9.4 (support students' learning).

whyNot.0: Sharps should not be passed hand to hand; the user disposes of them.
whyNot.1: Recapping is the hazard the regulations aim to remove; a one-handed technique does not make it compliant.
whyNot.2: Waiting leaves an ongoing injury risk; unsafe practice must be addressed at the time.

reteach.title: Who, what and when
reteach.question: If you remember one question for each law, which would it be?

blocks.body: HASAWA s7: am I taking reasonable care and cooperating? Manual handling: can I avoid it, and if not, have I assessed and reduced the risk? LOLER: is this hoist or sling in date and intact? COSHH: what does the assessment say about dilution and PPE? Sharps: am I disposing at the point of use, without recapping? RIDDOR: is it a death or specified injury (10 days) or more than 7 days off normal work (15 days)?

blocks.text: Fingers, thumbs and toes: a fracture there is NOT a specified injury. It only becomes reportable if the person is off normal work for more than 7 days.

explain.body: Every employee must take reasonable care for their own health and safety and for others affected by their acts or omissions, and cooperate with the employer so it can meet its duties.

test.q: A nurse notices that the ward's only hoist has a frayed sling. What does her duty under HASAWA s7 require?
options: Use the sling once more and report it at handover
Withdraw the sling, label it and report the fault
Tell the patient to stay in bed until next week
Repair the sling with tape until a new one arrives
test.why: Taking reasonable care for others means taking faulty lifting equipment out of use, labelling it so no one else uses it, reporting it and obtaining a safe replacement (HASAWA s7; LOLER).

whyNot.0: Using a damaged sling risks a fall and injury to the patient and staff.
whyNot.2: Confining the patient to bed is not a reasonable response when a replacement can be obtained.
whyNot.3: Improvised repairs are unsafe; lifting accessories must be examined and fit for use.

explain.body: Avoid hazardous manual handling, assess what cannot be avoided, reduce the risk. Lifting equipment for people (hoists and slings) needs a thorough examination at least every 6 months.

test.q: A hoist's examination label shows its last thorough examination was 8 months ago. What should the nurse do?
options: Use it, as the limit is 12 months
Use it with two staff present
Use it for transfers under 10 minutes
Take it out of use and report it
test.why: Hoists lift people, so they must be thoroughly examined at least every 6 months. An overdue hoist should not be used and should be reported (LOLER 1998).

whyNot.0: Twelve months applies to equipment that does not lift people.
whyNot.1: Extra staff do not make up for an overdue examination.
whyNot.2: Transfer duration does not affect the legal examination requirement.

explain.body: Deaths and specified injuries (for example fractures other than fingers, thumbs and toes) are reported without delay and within 10 days. Over-7-day injuries are reported within 15 days of the accident.

test.q: Which of these injuries to a member of staff is a RIDDOR specified injury?
options: A badly sprained ankle
A fractured big toe
A broken forearm
A deeply bruised knee
test.why: All fractures are specified injuries except those to fingers, thumbs and toes, so a fractured forearm is specified (HSE, RIDDOR 2013).

whyNot.0: A sprain is not on the specified injury list.
whyNot.1: Toe fractures are excluded from specified injuries.
whyNot.3: A bruise is not a specified injury.

explain.body: Follow the COSHH assessment and safety data sheet for any hazardous substance. For sharps: use safer devices as designed, do not recap, and dispose at the point of use as one unit.

test.q: Where should a nurse find the correct dilution and PPE for a new cleaning chemical?
options: On the ward's general daily cleaning rota
In its COSHH assessment and safety data sheet
From the last person who used the product
In the trust's manual handling policy document
test.why: COSHH requires an assessment with control measures; the COSHH assessment and safety data sheet state dilution, ventilation and PPE (HSE, COSHH basics).

whyNot.0: A cleaning rota shows who cleans and when, not how to control a hazardous substance.
whyNot.2: Word of mouth is not a controlled source of safety information.
whyNot.3: The manual handling policy covers moving loads, not chemicals.
